headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: LangGraph’s writable, networked orchestration can amplify Chatwoot customer data into uncontrolled downstream actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can expose customer messages and reports, while LangGraph can ingest application-defined files and stdin/stdout and run browser/tool nodes. A shared workspace or copied outputs create a plausible prompt-injection bridge, though no direct shared channel is documented. Uncertainty about the exact integration path pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Chatwoot outputs are copied into LangGraph prompts or files
IF LangGraph nodes parse Chatwoot content as instructions
IF a shared workspace or message queue is introduced between them
mitigations: Use a strict delimiter and instruction/data separation for all Chatwoot content
Add a content sanitizer before LangGraph ingestion
Disable automatic file-to-prompt loading
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to every Chatwoot artifact
requires-engineering: isolate the two agents in separate workspaces

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, messages, and reports; LangGraph has broad network egress plus filesystem read/write and can handle model-provider keys. If Chatwoot data is routed into LangGraph, the pair can exfiltrate sensitive customer content through networked tools by default. The blast radius is sensitive data leakage, not just a single document.
conditions: IF Chatwoot customer records are passed into LangGraph state or files
IF LangGraph tools forward that state to model providers or external APIs
IF both agents share an OS workspace or checkpointer-backed store
mitigations: Restrict LangGraph to redacted or synthetic data
Block outbound network access for runs handling Chatwoot data
Store Chatwoot artifacts in a separate, access-controlled workspace
requires-engineering: add field-level DLP before any LangGraph tool call
requires-engineering: segregate checkpointer storage by tenant and workflow

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot is a customer-support app with integrations, while LangGraph can execute shell, spawn subprocesses, run browsers, and write files. If both operate on the same workspace or shared state, LangGraph’s write and execution capabilities can overwrite or race with Chatwoot-managed artifacts. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so the conflict is dangerous by default once co-located.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or database
IF LangGraph nodes mutate files that Chatwoot also reads or writes
IF no external locking or transaction boundary is configured
mitigations: Separate writable directories for each agent
Disable LangGraph filesystem writes for shared artifacts
Add a lock around any shared database or file path
requires-engineering: move shared state behind transactional storage
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent namespaces in the checkpointer

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is explicitly a graph of nodes where each node may itself be an agent, and it can run developer-defined tools. If Chatwoot outputs customer facts or summaries into LangGraph without verification, LangGraph can treat them as authoritative and trigger downstream actions. That creates a classic unverified-output cascade with potentially irreversible external effects.
conditions: IF Chatwoot summaries are used as LangGraph node inputs
IF LangGraph nodes act on those inputs without a verification step
IF any downstream tool can send messages, update records, or invoke external APIs
mitigations: Insert a human review step before any action-taking node
Require schema validation on all Chatwoot-derived inputs
Mark Chatwoot outputs as untrusted in LangGraph prompts
requires-engineering: add provenance checks between nodes
requires-engineering: separate read-only analysis graphs from action graphs

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data and messages, while LangGraph handles model-provider API keys and broad network egress. The profiles do not specify residency or retention controls, so a compliance mismatch is plausible if customer data flows into LangGraph-backed providers or logs. I cannot prove a residency violation, so medium is the higher justified severity.
conditions: IF customer data from Chatwoot is sent to a non-approved model provider through LangGraph
IF LangGraph logs or checkpoints retain customer messages beyond policy
IF the deployment has residency or retention requirements
mitigations: Review provider and logging settings before processing customer data
Disable retention of raw Chatwoot payloads in checkpoints
Use a residency-approved model endpoint only
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing by data class
requires-engineering: implement deletion/export propagation across both systems
